Novartis, Bristol Myers Squibb, argenx and more have recently been hit with challenges as they attempt to advance assets targeting autoimmune diseases, with some programs being axed entirely while others were set aside for strategic reasons or paused over safety concerns.
Late this summer, Novartis and Bristol Myers Squibb paused trials of CAR T therapies in autoimmune conditions after patient deaths and safety signals, respectively. And they’re not the only ones facing challenges in this complex space, with several other companies suspending or ending development programs for clinical or strategic reasons.
This is somewhat to be expected, according to Matt Phipps, group head of biotechnology equity research at William Blair.
“The autoimmune disease field will always have some surprise setbacks,” Phipps told BioSpace in an email. Efficacy and safety are common culprits, he continued, pointing to other reasons such as the competitive environment, complexities of trial design and the biology underpinning the specific diseases.
Indeed, a key challenge for companies developing therapies for autoimmune diseases is how varied their patient pools are, said Graziano Seghezzi, managing partner and chief operating officer at Sofinnova Partners. Patients have different backgrounds and different disease presentations—and each one will respond differently to treatment.
“Many mild to moderate patients are decently controlled with low-cost drugs like rituximab or Humira,” meaning new treatments must be substantially better than these already effective therapies, Seghezzi told BioSpace in an email. “With a bar that high and Phase 3 so expensive, pharma uses Phase 2 as a go/no-go and stops early if there’s no strong efficacy signal or any safety signal.”
While strategic reasons factor heavily into companies’ decisions to discontinue programs, Seghezzi noted that science could also be a major driving force.
Truist Securities Managing Director Danielle Brill agreed. “Some autoimmune diseases are complex systemic diseases driven by multiple immune pathways, which creates several challenges for drug development,” she told BioSpace over email.
Brill offered Sjögren’s disease, a chronic condition where the immune system attacks the glands responsible for keeping the eyes and mouth moist, as an example. The disease also activates inflammatory cascades and causes the premature aging of stem cells in the salivary glands.
Argenx had hoped to address Sjögren’s with the under-the-skin FcRn inhibitor Vyvgart Hytrulo, which works by lowering the circulating levels of self-targeting IgG antibodies. Such a targeted approach, however, “may be unable to move the needle” in this disease, which is driven by more than just autoantibodies, Brill said. Indeed, argenx shuttered a Phase 3 study of the asset in Sjögren’s last month after a surprise futility finding.
Here, BioSpace looks at five recent high-profile setbacks for autoimmune disease drug developers.
Argenx ends Sjögren’s plans for Vyvgart Hytrulo
Argenx in October made the decision to discontinue development of Vyvgart Hytrulo in Sjögren’s disease after an independent data monitoring board during an interim review ruled that the drug would not meet the Phase 3 UNITY study’s primary endpoint of improvement in systemic disease. Once the study closes and the database is locked, argenx will conduct a full analysis of UNITY and share the findings to help inform future drug development for Sjögren’s.
Vyvgart Hytrulo, which was approved by the FDA in 2023 generalized myasthenia gravis and the following year for another autoimmune disease called chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, had shown promising signals for Sjögren’s disease. Data from the Phase 2 RHO trial, published in April, pointed to better disease outcomes in patients treated with argenx’s subcutaneous injection versus placebo, though this mid-stage trial was underpowered to detect a significant treatment effect, according to William Blair.
UNITY’s failure removes “the next potential blockbuster expansion opportunity” for Vyvgart Hytrulo, the analysts wrote in an Oct. 8 note. The firm had modeled peak sales of $1.4 billion in this indication.
Vyvgart Hytrulo in August cleared a Phase 3 study for autoimmune myositis. Argenx also has ongoing programs for efgartigimod—Vyvgart Hytrulo’s active ingredient—for Graves’ disease, systemic sclerosis and immune thrombocytopenia, among others.

Deaths, durability questions put Artiva into survival mode
Last month, Artiva Biotherapeutics disclosed two patient deaths and noted questions about the clinical response durability of its lead allogeneic cell therapy AlloNK—prompting the biotech to cut 94% of its employees.
Artiva, which had $319.1 million in cash, cash equivalents and investments as of Sept. 30, is now in survival mode, seeking out strategic opportunities that could include the sale or licensing of its assets, a merger with another company or an outright dissolution of the business.
AlloNK is natural killer cell therapy designed to be available off the shelf. Artiva was studying the asset in combination with rituximab in a Phase 2a basket trial in B cell–driven autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren’s disease and systemic sclerosis.
One patient in this trial developed a neurological complication that proved fatal. An independent safety review board, as well as the study investigator, deemed the death related to the chemotherapy regimen used to deplete patients’ white blood cells in preparation for the cell therapy. The second death was determined to be unrelated to AlloNK or any other component of the regimen.
Aside from these safety signals, long-term data revealed at the time showed that despite initial deep B cell depletion, AlloNK plus rituximab did not show the durable clinical response that Artiva was looking for. The biotech has therefore decided to discontinue the mid-stage study for AlloNK and will forego a planned Phase 3 study.

Novartis, BMS pause CAR T programs after deaths, safety signals
Also reporting fatalities were Novartis and Bristol Myers Squibb, both of which are looking to address autoimmune diseases with CAR T therapies.
In late August, news broke that three patients treated with Novartis’ rapcabtagene autoleucel (rap-cel), an investigational CD19-targeting medicine, developed serious hyperinflammatory complications that proved fatal, a company spokesperson told BioSpace at the time. The deaths prompted the pharma to suspend a clutch of immunology and neurology studies for rap-cel, including the Phase 2 AUTOGRAPH trials in autoimmune diseases including systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies.
“It’s absolutely our goal to get these trials started again,” Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan told reporters last month during a press call to present the pharma’s third quarter earnings report. There have been no new safety events flagged, he added.
At the same time, BMS revealed it had voluntarily suspended certain studies of its own CD19 CAR T therapy zolacabtagene autoleucel (zola-cel), being tested for various autoimmune diseases, such as myasthenia gravis and multiple sclerosis. The pharma had not detected any deaths at the time and was acting “out of an abundance of caution,” a spokesperson told BioSpace via email.
Two months later, however, BMS reported that one patient died after receiving zola-cel. The patient, who had highly active relapsing multiple sclerosis, was participating in a Phase 1 study and developed septic pneumonia 44 days after infusion with the cell therapy. There have been no other deaths across zola-cel’s autoimmune development program, BMS said in a press release at the time.

BMS reveals death from septic pneumonia of multiple sclerosis patient in CAR T trial
The disclosure—which came ahead of a presentation of data from the Phase 1 Breakfree-2 study at the ACTRIMS-ECTRIMS meeting—follows Bristol Myers Squibb’s late summer revelation that it had paused certain trials of zolacabtagene autoleucel.

Novartis ends lupus nephritis aspirations for Fabhalta
Novartis’ second showing on this list involves complement blocker Fabhalta , which is approved for IgA nephropathy, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and C3 glomerulopathy.
Novartis was looking to expand Fabhalta into lupus nephritis, a type of lupus that afflicts the kidneys. But in October, the pharma pulled the plug on a mid-stage study in this indication, a move that was driven by “strategic considerations” and not safety or interim efficacy findings, a company spokesperson told BioSpace at the time.
The pharma had completed the first part of the Phase 2 study —which combined Fabhalta with standard of care and compared the regimen against placebo plus standard of care—but decided not to push through with the next stage of the study. The second part of the trial was supposed to compare Fabhalta plus standard of care, Fabhalta plus placebo and placebo plus standard of care. Both parts were primarily testing for complete renal response by 24 weeks.
Novartis will continue studies of the drug in other indications, the spokesperson said. These include two Phase 3 trials in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome—one of which is set for a readout in 2028—and a late-stage study in generalized myasthenia gravis, with data expected next year.
Fabhalta made $505 million for Novartis in 2025, a 290% year-on-year jump.

Novartis ends mid-stage Fabhalta study in lupus, insists no efficacy or safety issues
Novartis will continue to study Fabhalta in other indications, with late-stage studies in two rare diseases—atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and generalized myasthenia gravis—expected to read out later this year and next year, respectively.

Pfizer’s strategic cull claims program for rare blood disorder
Like Novartis, Pfizer recently made a strategic call to end a mid-stage autoimmune study, this one testing the CXCR5 therapy PF-06835375 for primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). The discontinuation was “due to a business decision,” according to a federal clinical trials database , and was not linked to “any safety concerns.”
The Phase 2 study was testing four doses of PF-06835375 in patients with moderate to severe primary ITP, a rare blood disorder that develops when the immune system attacks platelets in the blood, in turn preventing the body from forming blood clots. Patients with this disorder bruise and bleed easily; if left unchecked, the disease can trigger serious complications such as hemorrhages. Before being wound down, the trial had enrolled 61 patients.
PF-06835375 works by targeting the CXCR5 protein , which is found on B cells and plays a part in their migration toward and positioning within the body’s lymphatic system; certain autoimmune diseases can arise when CXCR5’s activity is dysregulated. Phase 1 data published in 2024 showed dose-dependent reductions in B cells and follicular helper T cells following PF-06835375 treatment in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis.
PF-06835375 no longer appears on Pfizer’s pipeline page , nor is it listed in the company’s latest quarterly presentation .

Native YouTube App Lands on CarPlay With Open-Source Project
14 photos
Photo: GitHub
People have been asking for a way to watch YouTube on Android Auto and CarPlay for quite some time, and while third-party methods have existed for a while, an official YouTube app for cars is still nowhere to be seen.
That’s changing today with the release of YouDash, also referred to as YouTube Car, an open-source project whose purpose is to enable the native YouTube app on CarPlay.
Documented on GitHub , this application allows users to watch their favorite videos directly on their infotainment screens. Obviously, you’re only supposed to do this while the vehicle is parked for safety reasons, but the application will also work while you’re in motion. So before reading the rest of the article, just remember that this application must be used only while you’re stationary because otherwise, it would become a major distraction source in a second.
This app doesn’t come with any ads and promises a responsive feed, an on-screen keyboard, and a split-screen interface that allows the video to play on the left and see the playlist on the right. YouTube users would certainly find this implementation familiar, as this is the same configuration available on YouTube in the browser.
One of the best things about YouDash is that it can run on pretty much any CarPlay screen, so it doesn’t matter how small or large the infotainment unit is because the application adapts to its dimensions, resolution, and form factor. However, the developer explains that not all these settings have been tested.
Photo: GitHub Worth knowing is that the app won’t run on CarPlay with an iPhone updated to the latest version of iOS. While it’ll work properly on iOS 27.0.1, it won’t do it on iOS 27.3. As I reported not long ago, some video apps that enabled YouTube on CarPlay - not necessarily using the native app but by relying on other methods - also stopped working after the release of the most recent iOS update .
As a result, you’ll need an older version of iOS if you want to run this app in your car.
As for the installation method, it’s not necessarily the most intuitive approach. The app is not available through the App Store - and there’s a good chance it’ll never be - and there is no IPA file to install it manually. You’ll need a developer account and a Mac to install it on your iPhone, at least for the moment, though the developer should certainly find a more straightforward way to do the whole thing.
The step-by-step installation guide is available on GitHub.
Photo: Apple via MacRumors YouTube on Android Auto and CarPlay While YouTube is not yet available on Android Auto and CarPlay, both Google and Apple have paved the way for enabling video apps on their phone projection systems.
Apple enabled video app support on CarPlay with the release of iOS 26.4, suggesting that video apps like YouTube would eventually be fully supported on the platform. This still doesn’t happen, with video apps allowing users to watch videos on CarPlay not allowed on the App Store. Methods to gain the same functionality are still available, though, and they continue to work even after the most recent iOS updates.
Meanwhile, Google is much closer to unlocking YouTube on Android Auto. The company promised this functionality in the spring of this year when it announced that new app categories would be unlocked on Android Auto, including video and browsers. YouTube was supposed to spearhead this new expansion, with the first users originally projected to get the update by the end of 2026.
Most recently, Google said that video apps would land on Android Auto soon , though no further specifics were provided. Similarly, methods to enable YouTube on Android Auto are still available, though without official support. Google has rarely blocked them.
Photo: Apple via MacRumors Once YouTube lands on Android Auto , users will be allowed to watch video apps on their infotainment screens as long as their vehicles are stationary. The video playback will end when the car starts moving, with the experience switching to an audio-only mode where you’re only allowed to listen to the audio track of a video.
This functionality will be offered only if the video apps support it. YouTube will require a Premium subscription to allow the audio mode.
Google hasn’t shared any ETA specifics, but the first beta users are expected to receive the video app support by the end of the year. If everything works properly and no major bugs block the production rollout, the first devices should start getting support for the YouTube app through Google Play Store updates in the first quarter of the next year.
Apple has so far remained tight-lipped on such details, but considering CarPlay updates are still tied to iOS releases, it could take a while until this feature goes live officially. If anything, it’s safe to assume that iOS 28 will include more features on this front.

TE Connectivity OCP Summit-26
At the 2026 OCP Global Summit, I had the chance to sit down with Brian Payne, Vice President of Product Management for the Digital Data Networks (DDN) business at TE Connectivity. Many of our readers will know Brian from his 26 years at Dell, but he had been at TE Connectivity for about a month when we spoke. TE’s booth was built around three interconnected system-level racks, an optical interconnect rack, a sidecar power rack, and a copper IT rack, so we walked through the high-speed connectivity, the power delivery, and why TE thinks its system-level approach matters as AI infrastructure scales. We previously published a short booth tour video on STHLabs that got a surprising amount of attention, so we figured we would follow it up with the interview we did while we were there.
As always, we lightly edited this for readability.
Brian Payne and TE Connectivity at OCP
Patrick Kennedy: Brian, could you tell us a little bit about yourself?
Brian Payne: Sure. First of all, thanks. It’s great to see you again. I am vice president of product management here at TE Connectivity. I’ve got a long history in this industry. I spent 26 years at Dell.
Patrick Kennedy: Could you give us a little bit of background about TE Connectivity?
Brian Payne: TE Connectivity is a very large organization that manufactures and provides connectivity across multiple industries. But one of the most exciting things we’re doing right now is in what we call DDN, our Digital Data Networks division. We have experienced massive growth over the last three years, all building out the AI infrastructure that’s powering everything we’re doing today. It’s an exciting space to be in, with tremendous upside ahead of us.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-25
Patrick Kennedy: As part of that, TE Connectivity is well known for its contributions to OCP.
Brian Payne: TE Connectivity has been a part of OCP since 2017, so very early days. And as you can imagine, look around us. OCP has just boomed in terms of growth. TE Connectivity is focused on power and connectivity across all domains in the AI infrastructure. We have made tremendous contributions, and there are some exciting ones we’re going to talk about today.
448G and Next-Generation Front-Panel Connectivity
Patrick Kennedy: You have some things in your hand that I think you are super excited about. Could you tell us what these are and show us a little bit?
TE Connectivity USFP 3D Print OCP Summit 2026 3 Large
Brian Payne: Absolutely. At TE Connectivity, we’re thinking about how we deliver power for the data center and how we connect it. With every chip innovation, more and more bandwidth is coming. How do you get that out of the compute tray, and how do you get it into the network? One of the challenges is getting to 448. There are a lot of thermal challenges and signal integrity challenges to balance, and there’s a push in the industry to find the right solution. I would say there are two competing models out there. There’s XPO, which is a large.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-18
Patrick Kennedy: And just to be clear here, these are 3D-printed models.
Brian Payne: The reason I’ve got a 3D-printed model is that just Monday of this week ( at the October 2026 OCP Summit ), in a partnership with NVIDIA and Cisco, we announced our new standard for getting to 448. That’s what I have in my hand right here. You will see that it’s a similar form factor to QSFP today. One of the things we’re trying to do is balance signal integrity, power delivery, and form factor, and not over-index on one or the other. We believe we have a winner.
TE Connectivity USFP 3D Print OCP Summit 2026 2 Large
When you talk about developing concepts, that’s exactly what we have here. The transceiver slides in, and we’ve got a unique way to compress it so that power delivery and signal integrity are handled separately. So our signal integrity is really, really strong. The design is also made so that, as we see the power of the transceiver escalate, we’ll be able to do cold plate liquid cooling to pull heat out of the system.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-33
Patrick Kennedy: When you say 448G, you’re talking about the SerDes and really the per-lane communication speed.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-38
Brian Payne: Absolutely.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-34
Patrick Kennedy: That’s a big deal when we start talking about things like picojoules per bit, or how much power it takes to move data. But there are also a number of enabling technologies beyond USFP that you have behind us. Maybe we should start with some of the copper over here.
Copper Backplanes and Midplanes
Brian Payne: One of the huge areas of breakthrough in the industry has been copper backplane technology, and a combination of copper backplanes as well as midplanes. What we have here is an example of a midplane design, where a compute sled slides in along with power delivery. By going with this midplane design, you’re able to separate compute from GPU and then easily connect those together through the midplane. Then on the back side, we’ve got copper backplanes. In terms of an unlock for these rack-scale solutions, it is a highly technical, highly engineered solution that we have to produce in massive volumes.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-21
TE is one of the only companies in the industry that’s able to do that. There are very few in the market, and we’re excited about that. We are focused from the chip all the way to the switch. We’ve got innovation in near-chip packaging. We’ve got innovation around optics. We’re thinking about front and back I/O connectivity and the cabling in between. We’ve got innovation and products across all of those that are being deployed today at massive scale.
Patrick Kennedy: One of the interesting things in AI deployments is just how many lanes of communication are happening in every single box in a rack. How do you make that, number one, not use too much power and not create too much heat, but then also make it reliable? I imagine that’s a lot of what TE Connectivity needs to work on.
Brian Payne: One of the things I’ve discovered, and it’s been a pleasant surprise coming into TE Connectivity, is the R&D on the front end. How do we get through the material science challenges and develop the parts necessary to unlock these massive increases in bandwidth, and then deal with all of the power that’s required to push these chips and push the data across the network?
Optics and Co-Packaged Optics
Patrick Kennedy: There are a number of technologies today focused on extending the usefulness of copper, but the next generation is really optics. I think you have a demo of that over here.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-1
Brian Payne: The main thing I would say here is that you can go back to 10 Gigabit Ethernet, when we said the end of copper was coming, and copper is still prevalent in the industry. That being said, optics is there and solving a very, very important challenge. This is part of how we’re pathfinding and investing ahead. Earlier this year, we acquired an optics company, RAM Photonics. We’re bringing that into the product portfolio, and we’re massively investing in optics, from co-packaged optics as well as co-packaged copper, to getting the optics out of the system. So we’ve got a number of investments and new capabilities emerging to support that.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-3
Patrick Kennedy: Folks have been talking about co-packaged optics in the industry for what feels like forever. What’s different about what’s happening today versus 10 years ago, when folks were saying, “Oh, we need co-packaged optics immediately”?
Brian Payne: I think it is the physics challenge, and how far you can route copper as we increase the number of lanes that are necessary. There is a point in time where we will have to make the pivot. I realize you could have said that 10 or 12 years ago, but it’s becoming more and more real as we face these challenges. That’s why our investment and productization are picking up in that space. But it’s not stopping our investment in copper, because copper is still the state of the art. It’s still important to deliver the outcomes our customers expect. That’s where we’ve got a dual investment.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-6
Patrick Kennedy: One of the things you’re showing in the booth is some of the innovation around co-packaged optics, with connectors that go into the chip package so that you can service them. That was something folks didn’t know how to do even five or six years ago, and it’s a new innovation to bring co-packaged optics to the mass market and actually deploy it.
Brian Payne: When these are deployed at scale, it’s not just about getting the signal across the line. It’s about how you think about the system-level design and the operation, and what this looks like at scale. So to your point, serviceability is a critical design vector that drives innovation. That’s part of the TE approach: how do we not just get the technology working, but do it in a way that will support the massive volumes this industry is driving?
Power: The Sidecar Power Rack and Horizontal Busbar
Patrick Kennedy: This is a power shelf and a power rack. Why do we have a power rack, with racks focused on data connectivity on either side?
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-9
Brian Payne: To deliver the performance the industry is driving for, a massive amount of power is required to power the chips, and then to power the switches that connect them together. We simply don’t have the power density today to fit all of that in one rack, and that led to the innovation we see today. We’re starting to see sidecar designs like what we have here, which is a full rack of power distribution and cooling capabilities on one side.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-27
Then on the back side, when we get around there, we’ve actually got a busbar that runs horizontally, which is unique in the industry. Nobody’s done that. We did it to solve a problem with one of our large customers, and to deliver power to the next rack, the IT rack, with the IT equipment, the compute sleds, and the switches. That’s a great example of us thinking whip to chip. How do we put together a practical solution that addresses the ever-growing thirst for more and more power?
Patrick Kennedy: One of the really interesting things there is that the density challenge is actually in the nodes, so that you can get the copper connectivity within a rack. It’s actually using power to solve a connectivity challenge. And one of the big innovations is moving that power out of the rack and figuring out how to get a lot of current back into it.
Brian Payne: Right. In this industry, we have talked about power constraints and half-full racks for years and years. We’ve talked about busbars, and none of that really took hold until the AI boom. That’s what led to the innovation where we are delivering liquid-cooled busbars that span the rack to deliver power across without having to amp up the current and the overall heat dissipation. It’s about finding that balance in power delivery, but doing it in an efficient way.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-16
The next frontier is high voltage. We’ve got pathfinding concepts on the back side here where we’re pushing towards 800 volt. That’s what’s going to be necessary to get to a megawatt of power at the rack level. So how do we solve practically for the limitations of today, and also prepare ourselves for the future?
800V and Rack-to-Rack Power
Patrick Kennedy: One of the cool things about 800 volt is that it provides a more efficient power distribution path, which means your data center is more efficient. But there are cool things you’re doing as well. That 800 volt busbar back there has liquid cooling.
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-28
Brian Payne: Absolutely. And there are even things we can’t show you yet. Getting to 800 volt, number one, we’re thinking about how you get 800 volt all the way from the source. Every conversion has losses associated with it. So how do we bring it from the busways down into the rack, and then deliver it efficiently across the rack? To run this efficiently, liquid cooling to pull heat out is a critical element, and it’s something we’ve solved and have deployed across the industry.
Patrick Kennedy: You have another solution, which is a big, giant rack-to-rack cable. Can you tell me a little bit about that?
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-30
Brian Payne: Part of the issue is that once you get the power down to the IT equipment and you need to span multiple racks, you have to have an efficient way to get it rack to rack if a horizontal busbar isn’t the optimal choice. That’s why we’ve got prototype rack-to-rack 800 volt cables on the back of the system.
Patrick Kennedy: And that prototype is another example of how TE Connectivity is doing pathfinding with the OCP community and with customers to figure out how to solve these practical challenges.
Brian Payne: Our customer engagement starts in our customers’ data centers and in their offices, but also at places like OCP, where you can see we’re just covered up with people coming by. That inspires thought, new ideas, and future innovation. It’s super important to be a part of this community, to get those ideas in, show people what we’re thinking, and then iterate and evolve the designs going forward.
Pathfinding and Manufacturing at Scale
Patrick Kennedy: Could you give us some sense of how TE Connectivity doesn’t just make products for standards, but actually contributes to the pathfinding behind a lot of what is used in OCP?
TE Connectivity OCP Summit-35
Brian Payne: Absolutely. I’ll take power as an example. We think whip to chip. We’re one of the few, if not the only, company focused on the entire power delivery of the AI infrastructure at the AI rack. That means we see the bottlenecks before they occur, and we’re able to project ahead. This week, biopharma companies including Biogen, Bristol Myers Squibb and Roche are in Boston with new data on their efforts to tackle Alzheimer’s disease.
This year’s Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference program offers a snapshot of the maturation of non-amyloid approaches to address the hard-to-treat neurodegenerative disease. Starting Monday, researchers will present data on a range of drug mechanisms, shedding light on how going after tau and other targets may allow physicians to attack Alzheimer’s disease (AD) from multiple angles in the years to come.
Biogen and Eisai’s Leqembi and Eli Lilly’s Kisunla have shown that anti-amyloid therapies can help patients with AD. But while these products slow disease progression, they do not stop it, and they and contain boxed warnings for amyloid related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), or brain swelling.
The 2026 CTAD program is interesting because it illustrates the shift from an amyloid focus to a diversity of mechanisms, said Aaron Burstein, head of search and evaluation at the Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation.
“Alzheimer’s disease is a complex disorder with complex, underlying, interrelated pathobiology,” Burstein told BioSpace . “Having therapeutics that can target these different pathologic events helps move us one step closer to where we may be able to, in a not-so-distant future, see more personalized medicine and combination therapy strategies to target the diverse aspects of the disease.”
Expanding the Alzheimer’s arsenal
As the conference kicks off on Monday afternoon, researchers will present the first efficacy and safety results from POLARIS-AD , a 52-week Phase 3 clinical trial that tested AriBio and Fosun Pharma’s PDE5 inhibitor AR1001 in patients with early Alzheimer’s. Research suggests inhibiting PDE5 provides neuroprotective effects by elevating levels of an intracellular messenger and increasing blood flow to the brain. Fosun paid $60 million upfront for an option on the drug candidate in May.
AriBio’s Phase 2 study missed its primary efficacy endpoints, which assessed symptoms after 26 weeks, showing no benefit over placebo on key scales measuring cognition and change in AD. However, researchers speculated that AR1001 could perform better in a longer trial and, as no ARIA or ARIA-like symptoms were observed, identified a role for the treatment in patients who may not tolerate or qualify for anti-amyloid therapies.
TD Cowen analyst Joseph Thome outlined the potential implications of the Phase 3 readout. “Any positive data would be eagerly received by the physician and patient community, and companies down the line could look at combination approaches in early AD patients with their own mechanisms under development,” Thome told BioSpace via email. “However, we will have to see how compelling the activity is from the study.”
On Tuesday, meanwhile, Biogen will share additional biomarker and clinical findings from its Phase 2 CELIA study , which tested the tau-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) diranersen in early Alzheimer’s. The company published topline data on the drug candidate in May and presented more results in July at the Alzheimer’s Association’s annual conference, during which Biogen touted “an unprecedented drop in tau” after 18 months—which correlated with slowing of clinical decline.
Alzheimer’s disease

Biogen’s drug missed the trial’s primary endpoint, however, which assessed dose response in change from baseline on a cognitive and functional impairment scale. Questions that Biogen may address at CTAD include why diranersen had an inverse dose-response, according to Guggenheim Securities analysts.
“I’m looking forward to data around the relationship at the individual patient level between changes in tau as they relate to clinical effect,” Burstein said. “The data will hopefully provide us with a little bit more insight into how Biogen is thinking about their Phase 3 trial and the ability to identify the patient subgroups that may respond better.”
The diranersen program is part of a broader push to bring tau therapies to market. Later in the week at CTAD, researchers will share Phase 1b data for Novartis’ anti-tau ASO, NIO752, and healthy volunteer data on Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals’ siRNA-based approach to silencing production of the protein. Voyager Therapeutics will present baseline characteristics of patients enrolled in a Phase 1/2 study of its anti-tau antibody, VY7523 , which targets the C-terminal region of tau.
Like AR1001, these tau programs—if ultimately successful—could capture market share by improving on the safety of anti-amyloid drugs. In a Sept. 21 note to investors, TD Cowen analysts said 88% of surveyed experts are likely to use a therapy that matches amyloid drugs’ efficacy while reducing ARIA-monitoring burdens.
Tackling Alzheimer’s psychosis
In recent notes to investors, analysts at BMO Capital Markets and Guggenheim named data on BMS’ muscarinic drug Cobenfy in Alzheimer’s psychosis among the CTAD readouts to watch. BMS, which will present on Wednesday morning, has teased lead-in data from the Phase 3 ADEPT-1 study and extension data from the Phase 3 ADEPT-3 trial. The CTAD data are “encouraging,” Cristian Massacesi, chief medical officer at BMS, said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last month.
BMO analysts are confident that Cobenfy will reduce psychosis symptoms, “given ADEPT-1 is open-label and muscarinic efficacy in reducing psychosis symptoms has been demonstrated in elderly patients,” according to an Oct. 29 note. The analysts are more interested in the tolerability of the regimen, which requires patients to take a lower dose of Cobenfy three times a day, as compared with twice daily at a higher dose for schizophrenia, the drug’s approved indication.
Neuroscience

Guggenheim analysts noted implications for MapLight Therapeutics , which is developing a Cobenfy rival, ML-007C-MA. Good tolerability and durable improvements on Cobenfy would de-risk the muscarinic mechanism ahead of MapLight’s Phase 2 readout, the analysts said. On the other hand, if Cobenfy does show the gastrointestinal and nervous system side effects seen in patients with schizophrenia, it “would strengthen MapLight’s differentiation case,” the analysts added. MapLight expects to publish data from its Phase 2 Vista trial in the second half of 2027.
Also in Alzheimer’s psychosis, Acadia Pharmaceuticals on Tuesday morning will present Phase 2 data on remlifanserin, a 5HT2A receptor inverse agonist. The trial missed its main goal of improving hallucinations and delusions but hit a secondary objective, and Acadia argued that the data support Phase 3 development, noting that the trial only “narrowly missed” the primary endpoint. With Acadia sharing the full Phase 2 data at CTAD, Guggenheim analysts are looking for details on whether remlifanserin’s effect scales with disease severity.
Enhancing anti-amyloid outcomes
Last but not least, developers of anti-amyloid drugs will share data on incumbent products and next-generation assets. On Monday evening, researchers will present five-year open-label extension data from the Clarity AD trial of Leqembi. The update will cover long-term clinical outcomes, disease progression and safety.
Meanwhile, several sessions will cover Roche’s development of trontinemab , which pairs the company’s Brainshuttle delivery technology with an anti-amyloid antibody. The company began Phase 3 trials of the drug candidate as an Alzheimer’s treatment last year.
A late Monday afternoon symposium will detail updated data from Roche’s Phase 1b/2a Brainshuttle AD study. In data presented last year at CTAD, more than nine in 10 patients treated with trontinemab tested negative for amyloid plaques.

During the same symposium, a presentation will feature the “first human imaging evidence on how much trontinemab reaches the brain and where it distributes,” Guggenheim analysts said. Roche has hypothesized that preferential targeting of plaques in functional tissue, with less engagement of vascular amyloid, may limit ARIA with edema, the analysts added. Imaging data could provide support for this hypothesis.
A separate presentation on Wednesday will highlight a Phase 3 Alzheimer’s prevention study of trontinemab, which is set to start this month.
While improving the delivery of anti-amyloid therapies remains a priority, drugs that clear the protein may only be part of the solution to Alzheimer’s. CTAD also features sessions on NLRP3, SEMA4D, BDNF and other targets.
Burstein sees the range of other targets being discussed at CTAD as essential, explaining that “we clearly need additional agents that target other mechanisms that could be used in combination to augment the efficacy.”

Honda Prelude Adds the Fancy Bordeaux Edition to the Lineup in Australia, Starting From $45k
11 photos
Photo: Honda
The Japanese automaker Honda has introduced a new special edition to its lineup in the Land Down Under, the cool-looking Honda Prelude Bordeaux Edition, which costs AU $67,000 driveaway, or about $45k at the current exchange rates.
The Asian carmaker is taking good care of its Australian market and announced quite a few novelties recently: it partnered with artist Kentaro Yoshida on a custom Honda Super-ONE for a set of fresh decals with a unique visual style by the acclaimed Japanese artist and illustrator; announced “the first vehicle of a new generation, (…) pointing to its future direction for design and innovation” with the all-new Honda Avancier ; revealed that its next-generation hybrid system will be called ‘Honda Hybrid,’ and more.
They also announced for both the Honda and Acura brands a massive 636k vehicle recall procedure to address an error with the Driver Attention Monitor road-condition compensation calculation, which can leave drivers without power steering assistance in case of a mishap, so it’s not all just roses and daffodils. Anyway, Honda Prelude fans, at least the ones living in Europe and in Australia, won’t complain much about issues because they’ll be rather busy pampering their new special edition vehicles.
Back in late September 2026, Honda announced a new Prelude Limited Edition – that’s the name, no fancy titles on these occasions – available across the Old Continent starting this fall season for the 2027 model year, and it was wearing a decidedly special hue mix. The red-on-red aesthetic is the Premium Crystal Garnet Metallic combined with a Bordeaux interior. Now, Australian fans don’t need to envy their European peer anymore.
That’s because the local division of Honda announced today, November 16, 2026, the introduction of a new Bordeaux Edition Prelude as a “striking new addition to the Prelude line-up following the model’s return earlier this year.” You guessed correctly: it’s also finished in Premium Crystal Garnet Red on the outside and features a “distinctive heritage-inspired interior,” so the Bordeaux Edition mirrors the model seen just a few weeks ago in Europe. We really hope that America is coming next because the Prelude looks great in this color combination.
Honda Australia welcomed the return of the iconic Prelude nameplate earlier this year, and the new Bordeaux Edition will try to make it a collectible, too, not just another cool sports car. So, aside from its bespoke Premium Crystal Garnet Metallic exterior, the new special edition also includes front and rear crimson accents, a front upper grille in the body color, red Brembo x Prelude brake calipers, and 19-inch black cut alloy wheels. Inside, the Bordeaux edition features exactly the name’s color, of course.
Additionally, the 2027 Honda Prelude gets a Black X Blue interior trim for the Black model and also a Red exterior color. Otherwise, it’s the same as before, sporting the new S+ Shift technology that helps simulate the sound and feel of rapid automatic gear changes – including “a ‘kick’ and rev-matching throttle ‘blip’ felt during gear changes and engine braking.” The powertrain of the sixth-gen Prelude is a 2.0-liter hybrid with 200 hp combined and a single-speed direct-drive transmission setup.

Starship's Most Ambitious Launch Yet, Flight 15, Ends With a Bittersweet Outcome
8 photos
Photo: SpaceX
Years of preparation and 14 previous test flights culminated this past weekend with Flight 15 of the SpaceX Starship. It was supposed to mark the first-ever double-catch of the booster and spacecraft in the arms of Mechazilla towers, but everything ended in a bittersweet manner as the mission was only partially accomplished.
Starship Flight 15 started on Friday, November 13, when launch pad 2 at the private space company's Starbase complex in Texas ignited its engines and departed the surface of the planet.
The mission was off to a pretty amazing start, with the Super Heavy booster meant to propel the spacecraft into orbit igniting all its 33 Raptor engines, thundering off the pad just as planned. It successfully completed its ascent and hot staging and then began its descent back to the place it had left only minutes before.
On its way down, the hardware seemed to be performing every single task perfectly. It went through the required directional flip maneuver and fired up 32 of its 33 engines once more (not a perfect outcome, but something that has happened before, and is a non-issue) for the boostback burn.
Photo: SpaceX For reasons that are still under investigation, but seem to have to do with low fuel mass, the hardware's guidance, navigation, and control systems decided it's not a good idea for the booster to get back to the pad, as intended. They triggered an automated abort sequence as the Super Heavy was coasting, diverting the hardware away from the pad and to an offshore location.
As expected, the rocket then executed a landing burn, slowing down its descent above the surface of the water, and, as it was hovering over the Gulf of Mexico, cut off its engines. Finally, the flight termination system kicked in, and the story of this Super Heavy ended in a spectacular explosion.
By all intents and purposes, this portion of the flight was a failure, as the booster was supposed to come back to the tower, as it had done three times before. Despite this, nobody considers the event to be a failure, as, if you really think about it, Flight 15 was more about the Starship. And that one performed flawlessly.
Following its separation from the Super Heavy, Starship moved on to Earth orbit by firing its six Raptor engines. It moved through a brief coast stage as it climbed, then fired up a single engine to perform its orbital insertion burn.
Photo: SpaceX For the second time in its history, the spacecraft made it to orbit, where it proceeded to deploy its cargo of 26 Starlink V3 satellites. The deployment went without a hitch, and, SpaceX says, contact with the satellites was quickly established, and they began raising their orbits to become part of the constellation.
Once this part of the flight was complete, Starship was not left with much more to do, but, as teams on the ground sought to test pretty much all of the onboard systems (engines, comms systems, flight computers, navigation sensors, and structural integrity), it spent no less than 20 hours in orbit – the longest it has stayed up there so far.
When everything was said and done, Starship began its return to the launch pad , relighting a single Raptor engine to perform a de-orbit burn. It then made its way back to the surface, following a path that took it over some populated areas in northern Mexico and southern Texas, but around the major cities of the Rio Grande Valley.
As it approached, it performed a final swoosh maneuver and fired up three of its engines to slow its descent. In a perfect return, it flipped and slowly positioned itself directly in the two metal arms of the Mechazilla tower, which grabbed hold of it and secured it for the first time ever.
Photo: SpaceX From start to finish, Starship's Flight 15 spent 22.5 hours on the job, and, even if it hasn't ended in a demo of full reusability, it is considered by SpaceX a defining moment that changed everything.
Catching a spacecraft in a tower is something that no one has ever done before, and effectively puts SpaceX on the path not only to full reusability for the booster and Starship, but also on the path to fulfilling its role in the Artemis Moon exploration program, the stepping stone to humanity's first crewed mission to Mars .
In the days to come, we expect Elon Musk's space company to reveal what went wrong with the Super Heavy return and imagine a fix for it. It's too early to tell when Flight 16 will take place, but it's more than obvious it will build on the successes (and failures) of this one, and will try to be remembered as the first time an entire orbital system of this size is recovered in working order. BridgeBio has produced two young leaders on BioSpace’s 2026 40 Under 40 list. Morgan Paull and Christine Zhang attribute their early success to the company’s unique hub-and-spoke model and a drive to help patients with few treatment options. “It’s very personal,” Paull said.
Christine Zhang and Morgan Paull didn’t walk a typical path to reach their place on BioSpace ’s 2026 40 Under 40 list. That’s at least partly because the company they share in common—BridgeBio Pharma—is anything but typical.
The California-based biotech—which develops treatments for rare, genetic conditions—functions under a hub-and-spoke model, with teams operating autonomously as individual spokes, according to its website, while central hubs provides clinical, regulatory and commercial capabilities and expertise.
“In a model like ours, it’s kind of like you get to be the starting quarterback from very early on,” Paull, now chief operating officer at new BridgeBio hub company GondolaBio, told BioSpace .
Morgan Paull, chief operating officer, GondolaBio
When Paull started at BridgeBio—the original hub—in 2020, he had an opportunity to consider strategy setting, something you normally don’t get to think about until you’ve had a long career in a specific functional area. “It’s been transformative for me.”
Zhang, who serves as executive director and program lead at BridgeBio spoke company Evanesco Therapeutics. “The word that comes to mind for me is intrapreneurship,” she told BioSpace , referring to internal entrepreneurs. “It’s really because you have so much autonomy and ownership over your work, and you’re able to have a tremendous impact much earlier in your career.”
Launched in 2024, GondolaBio—like BridgeBio—is focused on rare disease. The young biotech conducts early-stage research and development for genetic diseases. Under the BridgeBio umbrella, GondolaBio has “a lot of shared DNA [and] some shared services,” Paull explained. BridgeBio founder and CEO Neil Kumar also serves as executive chair of GondolaBio.
Meanwhile, Zhang—a former investment banker—joined BridgeBio in 2021, working on therapies for transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), before she came up with an idea for a brand-new drug for the cardiovascular disease, an amyloid depleter. “BridgeBio was very supportive of that, so I spun off Evanesco, and we have our own in-house discovery molecule that we’re taking to the clinic,” she said. Evanesco also operates under the BridgeBio umbrella.
Christine Zhang, executive director and Evanesco Therapeutics program lead, BridgeBio
Noting that BridgeBio did not have a depleter for ATTR-CM in house, Zhang spent hours “really getting obsessed with this space,” after which she put together a pitch deck to bring to Kumar requesting funding for the new affiliate. Kumar gave her the opportunity to present to the company’s board, saying, “I’ll give you one hour; if you can convince them that this is a good idea, then the money is yours.”
“Fortunately, it went well,” she said, and Evanesco was born.
Unlike the stabilizers currently on the market—such as Pfizer’s tafamidis and BridgeBio’s own Attruby —amyloid depleters for ATTR-CM have the potential to reverse the disease, Zhang explained.
“Our goal is to go beyond what the current therapies see right now, which is halt the disease, but to take that one step further and potentially actually undo past symptoms of disease and potentially lead to disease reversal,” she added. Evanesco hopes to be in the clinic with this molecule in 2027 or 2028.

There is a rare disease ethos in the BridgeBio family of companies—which also includes BridgeBio Oncology Therapeutics (BBOT)—that drives leaders like Zhang and Paull.
For Zhang, the rare disease community is unique; many of the conditions are so rare, they are unknown even to physicians.
“When we interact with patients and patient communities, it is so meaningful because there is such a strong sense of connection when they find each other,” she said, adding that she sees this playing out in ATTR-CM, which affects around 13,500 people in the U.S. “Patients help each other out by referring physicians or discussing treatment options, and they are always so excited and grateful and appreciative of the work that we do in drug discovery.”
Zhang shared that Evanesco was inspired by a comment she heard during a patient advocacy meeting, with someone saying, “All these existing treatments are great, but what we really want is a depleter.”
“We really have the patients driving forward our science and our focus,” she said.
“It’s motivating to work on any medicine for patients in need, but it’s a lot more personal in the case of rare disease,” Paull agreed. “If it’s 2 a.m. and I’m working and would like to be asleep,” he’ll think about the middle-schooler with hereditary pancreatitis who has been in the hospital every month this year, or the middle-aged woman with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP)—a rare disorder that causes painful sensitivity to the sun—who wasn’t diagnosed until the age of 40.
EPP—which has a patient population of around 25,000 across the U.S. and Europe, according to GondolaBio—is the biotech’s lead indication , with the candidate PORT-77 currently in Phase 2 testing . GondolaBio also has a Phase 1 program in recurrent oxalate kidney stones, along with investigational new drug–enabling studies in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A, the genetic disease alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
Paull told another story, about an 18-year-old patient with a plexiform neurofibroma—a tumor condition commonly caused by neurofibromatosis type 1—an indication for which GondolaBio is in lead optimization.
The morning of his interview with BioSpace , Paull was texting back and forth with this young patient about the music that he likes, which, he said, is country. “It’s very personal,” Paull said. “I think about those specific people.”

Next-Gen 2028 Audi RS6 Avant Getting a US Visa, V8 Power Is Likely – Report
7 photos
Photo: SH Proshots
It’s been more than one and a half years since Audi introduced the latest generation A6. The model was supposed to be christened the A7 as per the brand’s new naming scheme, but the automaker eventually changed its mind.
The reason was that it would have been too confusing for its clientele, though as per the initial plan, Audi was supposed to use even numbers on EVs and odd numbers on ICE-powered cars. And that is precisely why there is no new A4, as the model has become the A5. However, that could change when the mid-cycle refresh arrives, with an obvious emphasis on the word “could,” because the rumor mill hints that the new A5 could be rechristened the A4.
Now, the new-gen Audi A6 may be alive and kicking, but the automaker has yet to introduce its range-topping version. We are talking about the RS 6, which will be offered as a four-door sedan and a five-door station wagon. The former is joining the lineup after a very long wait, because the last RS 6 Sedan was offered for the C6 generation, which was made between 2007 and 2011, based on the VW Group’s C6 platform shared with the lesser S6, A6, and A6 allroad quattro from that era.
The next-generation Audi RS 6 lineup, on the other hand, will utilize the PPC (Premium Platform Combustion. This architecture is the foundation stone not only of the latest A6 family, but also the smaller A5 (B10), and the Mk3 Q5. The new Q7 is also based on this construction, and so is the first-ever Q9, because Audi now has a rival to the likes of the Mercedes GLS, BMW X7, and other full-size crossovers.
Photo: SH Proshots We have seen images of scooped prototypes , which have been joined by all kinds of renderings trying to decipher what it will look like beneath the skin, and it seems that not a single week can usually go by without the next-gen Audi RS 6 making its way to our news feed. The latest information about it came via one of the company’s execs, and it is all about whether the model will reach our shores or not in its long-roof configuration. And the answer is simple: yes!
In a quick sitdown with TheDrive, Audi of America’s Senior Vice President of Product Management, Filip Brabec, was asked whether the all-new Audi RS 6 Avant will come to the United States or not, to which he answered: “If there is globally an RS 6 Avant, then it will come to America.” And there indeed is one, as we have witnessed it multiple times. So, there you have it, folks, official confirmation that the model will take on the likes of the BMW M5 Touring as well on our shores, not only the M5 Sedan.
Its biggest rival in the segment has 717 hp (535 kW /727 ps) and 738 lb-ft (1,000 Nm) of torque to play with from its plug-in hybrid 4.4-liter twin-turbo V8 engine, enabling 0-60 mph (97 kph) in 3.4 seconds for the Sedan and 3.5 seconds for the Touring. But what exactly will power the all-new Audi RS 6 lineup? Contradicting reports speak about either a V6 or a V8, with electric assistance and twin turbocharging.
If it is the former, then it will likely be the mill used on the new RS 5. And that’s a 2.9-liter twin-turbo V6 making 503 hp (375 kW/510 ps), with the electric motor generating 174 hp (130 kW/177 ps). The total output is rated at 630 hp (470 kW/639 ps), and 0-62 mph (100 kph) is a 3.6-second affair. But if this setup will indeed make its way to the upcoming RS 6, then expect a lot more power, as the model needs to be faster than its predecessor, as it will take an inevitable swing at the BMW M5.
Photo: SH Proshots The previous Audi RS 6 Avant had 621 hp (463 kW/630 ps) to play with from its twin-turbo 4-liter V8, hitting 62 mph (100 kph) in a little over three seconds, and maxing out at 155 mph (250 kph). Some say that a plug-in hybrid V8 could be what powers the upcoming generation, and it could be the setup used on the Bentley Continental GT Speed, which has 771 hp (575 kW/782 ps) available via the right pedal in total.
The quoted outlet expects the all-new Audi RS 6 Avant (and Sedan) to feature a plug-in hybrid V8 assembly, and the model will have a smooth- and quick-shifting eight-speed automatic transmission and the mandatory quattro all-wheel drive system. It will be interesting to learn whether it will indeed be faster than its predecessor, in a straight-line sprint, anyway, because the electric assistance has made it a lot heavier. And let’s not forget than the new BMW M5 is slower than the old one.
Pretty much everything goes at this point when it comes to the performance, as well as the chosen powertrain, and deep down, we hope that the new Audi RS 6 will indeed feature a V8 and not a V6, and that it will be faster than the old one. Everything will be revealed in due course, and we will likely have to wait a few more months before seeing it with no camo in an official environment, as the unveiling should take place in 2027, and the vehicle should go on sale for the 2028 model year in USA.

BMW's Latest Water Pump Fire Recall Covers 720,000 Vehicles and Comes With a "Park Outside" Advisory
9 photos
Photo: BMW
BMW is recalling a massive 720,796 vehicles in the United States market for water pump connectors that may short circuit, increasing the risk of a fire. Even though lab tests found embrittlement and cracks in the electrical connector's material, the Bavarian automaker still hasn't identified the root cause.
26V733 is what the federal watchdog calls this campaign, which also comes with a "park outside" advisory due to the fire risk. Customers are urged to park away from buildings and other vehicles until dealers complete the repair.
This recall started with an older campaign, specifically 24V608 from August 2024. Back in April 2025, the German manufacturer learned of a thermal overload incident at the water pump connector in a 5 Series from a non-US market. Preliminary data showed that the subject vehicle had received the previous remedy, which is why BMW hypothesized an improper repair.
In June 2025, a US-market 3 Series that also received the earlier remedy developed smoldering at the subject connector. Laboratory work supported the possibility of an improper repair, but nevertheless, BMW decided to broaden its investigation. A January 2026 review of field data identified additional cases of overheating and thermal overload after the 24V608 remedy.
BMW naturally collected water pumps that showed signs of damage, and the supplier joined the party in February 2026. Pierburg Pump Technology GmbH is the supplier in question, which identified possible leak paths around the electrical connector in March 2026. This, in turn, prompted both parties to turn their attention to the electrical connector's PBT material.
Photo: BMW Testing found severe embrittlement of the polybutylene terephthalate material, but alas, no root cause had been established. Further tests in April 2026 found that embrittlement affected specific areas of the connector, while in-depth analyses confirmed some cracks for good measure. An outside expert was brought in back in May 2026, with all three parties considering hydrolysis of the PBT as a possible explanation.
In this context, hydrolysis stands for the chemical breakdown of the polyester polymer in the connector. Even a tiny fraction of hydrolysis can compromise the material, turning the plastic brittle. So far, BMW is aware of 10 incidents in the US market involving vehicles repaired under the previous recall.
The vehicle population includes older Bimmers, including the 2012 through 2016 model year Z4. Affected nameplates further include the 3 Series, 4 Series, and 5 Series, X1, X3, X4, and X5, plus the 2 Series Coupe and Convertible. The largest groups are the 3 Series and X3, totaling 236,702 and 163,727 units, respectively.
Curiously enough, BMW has not finished developing the new remedy. Once it becomes available, dealers nationwide will carry out the repair at no charge to affected customers. And once said remedy becomes available, customers who paid for related work may qualify for reimbursement as long as they provide adequate proof of payment.
Dealers have already been notified of 26V733, but customers will have to wait until December 25, 2026, to receive mailed notifications. Indeed, the recall documentation lists Christmas Day as the interim notification date.

How India and other emerging hubs for drug development can be key to reshaping medical costs globally.
Every breakthrough therapy creates two fundamental questions: Can we develop it? And once we do, can society afford it? For decades, biotechnology has focused primarily on answering the first. Today, as scientific advances accelerate and the economics of innovation change, the second is becoming equally important.
Across my experience in my current role as founder and CEO of Eyestem and my previous stint as CEO of IQVIA’s Cenduit, it’s become increasingly clear to me that the next era of biotechnology must deliver breakthroughs that can be developed and deployed sustainably at scale.
This is where emerging biotech hubs can play a transformative role.
Societies are aging, meaning the prevalence of chronic and degenerative diseases is increasing. At the same time, government debt is mounting, so funding rising healthcare costs will become increasingly difficult. Layer onto that the high cost of many new treatments such as cell and gene therapies—which are often priced in the millions of dollars—and the fact that these novel modalities are moving beyond rare diseases and toward conditions affecting much larger populations.
Current estimates suggest it takes more than $1.5 billion to develop an innovative drug. While drugmakers have traditionally followed the playbook of high stakes innovation yielding high rewards, we’re now facing a fundamentally different economic challenge—one that emerging biotech hubs may be best suited to address.
For years, countries such as India and China were viewed primarily as cost-efficient destinations for manufacturing, clinical research and outsourcing. As both countries continue to grow and develop a large, aspirational middle class, they are gradually yet persistently moving up the value chain.
China is increasingly demonstrating that world-class biotechnology innovation can be developed at significantly lower cost points. India, already a global leader in vaccine and biologics manufacturing, is well positioned to extend this strength into advanced therapies such as cell and gene therapy. Combined with its scientific talent, growing biotechnology ecosystem and digital infrastructure, the country has the potential to follow China’s trajectory.

To grow into a biopharma juggernaut, China aims to become the leading source of innovative medicines on the global markets—a goal that experts say the country is on track to hit.

Starting a company in India
The above thesis led us to start Eyestem in India in 2015. The purpose of Eyestem is to create innovative therapies for incurable, complex diseases with large patient populations at a price point that is accessible for a large section of humanity. The intent was to build on several such successes such at the $10 Intra-ocular lens built by Aravind Eye Hospitals.
Consider the contrast between Luxturna, developed by Spark Therapeutics for a rare inherited retinal disease affecting fewer than 1 million people and priced at around $495,000 per vial, and Eyecyte-RPE, our retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell suspension therapy currently in Phase 2 trials for geographic atrophy, a disease that affects more than 200 million people worldwide. We are targeting a price point of around $95,000. Even if the cost per treatment were similar, the financial implications of treating millions of patients would be vastly different. The reduction in cost per product would have to be orders of magnitude more for it to be widely accessible and affordable.
The opportunity is not simply to offer lower costs. It is to create an innovation advantage—the ability to discover, develop, test and manufacture breakthrough therapies more efficiently, while maintaining scientific and regulatory standards.
Emerging biotech hubs are uniquely positioned because they can redesign the entire innovation process rather than simply replicate Western models. They combine strong scientific talent, lower development costs, digital-first infrastructure, increasing biologics manufacturing capability and rapidly maturing regulatory ecosystems. Newer ideas, like the 15-year mega grants that China has announced for its scientists and the approximately $12 billion Research and Development Innovation fund that India has announced are just the kind of initiatives that will allow for step change in progress.
But technology alone will not be enough. The ecosystem around innovation must evolve as well.
The shift from cost advantage to innovation advantage is already underway. Biotech hubs that embrace it will reap the lion’s share of the benefits.
Regulatory pathways, particularly for early-stage clinical trials, need to become more streamlined without compromising safety or scientific integrity. There is encouraging movement in the U.S., while Japan and China have demonstrated more adaptive approaches in the cell therapy space. Europe, despite its scientific strengths, has generally moved more cautiously and could benefit from greater regulatory agility. Emerging hubs can decisively take a lead in this area by offering expedited approvals within a few defined centers of excellence.
Innovators must also be prepared to rethink pricing, while healthcare systems and insurers must assess therapies based on their lifetime value for patients and healthcare systems—not simply their initial price. Newer financing models that can offset high upfront financial shock for patients may become necessary especially as fewer patients are reported to be filling scripts . Because emerging hubs offer a significant cost advantage of production, they would be a great test bed for such new pricing paradigms between governments, insurers and patients before they are launched in developed markets.
Governments, meanwhile, should incentivize affordable innovation—emphasis on affordable. Policies that encourage companies to reduce the cost and complexity of developing breakthrough therapies could have as much societal impact as incentives for discovery itself. As financial resources become scarce, governments will be taking a much closer look at the return on investment from such innovation. The recent move by the U.S. government to create a Most Favored Nation policy linking prices to other country benchmarks is a step in this direction. Expect more of these going forward.
The future of biotechnology will depend on more than our ability to invent breakthrough therapies. It will depend on our ability to make them economically sustainable and accessible to the populations that need them most.
Emerging biotech hubs have a unique opportunity to lead this transformation. Their competitive advantage should no longer be defined simply by lower costs but by their ability to build integrated ecosystems.
The shift from cost advantage to innovation advantage is already underway, and the biotech hubs that embrace it will not merely participate in the future of global drug development. They will help lead the next wave of innovation and reap the lion’s share of the benefits.
